tasks.title: Listening 2 — Interview

items.stem: When did preparation begin?
How long did the team work?
Who helped organise the captions?
What languages were used in the captions?

tasks.transcript:
Interviewer: Welcome to our school identity programme. What encouraged you to make a personal photo board, Huda?
Huda: I noticed that classmates who seemed different often shared hobbies, so I wanted to help people discover them.
Interviewer: Did the first display focus only on people's appearance, or did you include their interests as well?
Huda: We included their hobbies, family traditions and personal strengths. Appearance cannot explain the whole story of someone's identity.
Interviewer: Where did your team first collect information for the project?
Huda: We visited three classes and offered simple questionnaires. Everyone was free to answer privately or leave a question blank.
Interviewer: When did you begin preparing the photographs?
Huda: We started in October and worked for nearly three weeks before the first display was ready.
Interviewer: Who helped you organise the captions, and which languages did you decide to use?
Huda: Our English teacher helped us. We wrote short captions in both Arabic and English so more families could understand.
Interviewer: Did you keep the photograph when one classmate changed her mind about showing it?
Huda: No. We removed her picture immediately and used a drawing instead. Respecting someone's choice matters more than a display.
Interviewer: How did the project change the way students talked to one another at school?
Huda: People began asking about interests rather than making quick assumptions. Several shy pupils also joined clubs that suited them.

tasks.title: Reading 2 — Short answers
tasks.passage:
Many schools organise exhibitions about personal identity. Supporters say these projects help young people discover what they have in common, even when their backgrounds or personalities are different. Aisha, who enjoys studying astronomy in the evening, joined a project after moving to a school in Sohar. Her friend Salma offered to design the posters, and together they prepared a model of the solar system. Such activities can encourage new friendships and allow students to share their interests.

A further advantage is that students can contribute in different ways. Hamad felt confident speaking to visitors, while Noura preferred organising details quietly. In my opinion, both roles are valuable because a successful exhibition requires careful preparation as well as clear presentations. Aisha now understands that identity includes values, habits, interests and the way people treat others, not just appearance or nationality.

However, identity projects also have disadvantages if they are badly managed. Pupils may feel uncomfortable sharing personal photographs or family information. Others might make unfair assumptions about someone based on a single hobby. Teachers should therefore ask for permission, offer alternatives such as drawings and make sure that every student can refuse to share private details.

Overall, I believe these exhibitions are beneficial when participation is respectful and voluntary. Listening first is helping Aisha develop the skill of understanding other people. An exhibition should encourage questions and kindness rather than pressure pupils to explain every part of their lives. Students are likely to learn more when different strengths receive equal recognition.

tasks.transcript:
Interviewer: Today we are discussing how young people can protect languages and share stories. Why did your class begin this project, Bilal?
Bilal: We realised that some children understood their grandparents' words but rarely tried speaking the same language themselves.
Interviewer: Were you studying only written words, or were you interested in conversations and stories as well?
Bilal: We focused on conversations. A language lives through the people who use it and tell stories in it.
Interviewer: Where did your first interview take place?
Bilal: We recorded our first interview at the community centre with my grandmother, who loves telling family stories.
Interviewer: What happened while you were checking the recording, and how did your team respond to the problem?
Bilal: The microphone stopped working for a few minutes. We checked the batteries and repeated that section patiently.
Interviewer: What language did the grandparents speak during the interview?
Bilal: They spoke Arabic, and two pupils added short English summaries so the whole class could learn from them.
Interviewer: When did you share the collection?
Bilal: We shared it on Tuesday during the school exhibition, but we used only recordings that families had approved.
Interviewer: What was the most important lesson you learned about communication through this project?
Bilal: Listening respectfully is as important as speaking clearly. We should ask questions instead of pretending we understand.

tasks.title: Reading 2 — Short answers
tasks.passage:
School films can be an effective way to explore how communication has changed. Supporters believe that interviewing different generations gives students practical experience of listening, speaking and checking evidence. Mariam's class made a short film about communication in their town. They interviewed grandparents about letters and younger people about messaging apps. In my view, bringing these perspectives together was more useful than simply listing modern devices.

One advantage of such projects is that students learn how quickly misunderstandings can happen. During editing, a recorded interview seemed to disappear from the shared folder. Bilal had moved it to protect it from accidental changes, but he forgot to inform the team. His decision was sensible in one respect, yet the lack of explanation worried his classmates. This incident shows that even helpful actions can create problems when messages are incomplete.

On the other hand, making a film can be difficult. Recordings might contain private details, translations may be inaccurate and classmates may disagree about what to include. Teachers should check that speakers have given permission and encourage pupils to compare summaries with the original recordings. Students also need time to review subtitles and make sure their message is clear to different audiences.

I think the benefits of a carefully planned communication film outweigh these difficulties. Mariam's team agreed to keep a record of file movements in future so that everyone could find important materials. The finished project taught them that reliable communication is not only about technology or speed. It also requires honesty, patient listening and respect for the person receiving a message.

tasks.title: Listening 2 — Interview

items.stem: Who suggested the invention?
What activates the reminder?
Where will students test the prototype?
What problem was found in the early version?
When is the next meeting with the engineer?

tasks.transcript:
Interviewer: Welcome to Future Voices. What kind of technology is your science club developing, Noura?
Noura: We are building a simple device that reminds older people to drink water at regular times during the day.
Interviewer: Did the idea come from a famous inventor, or did someone in your local community suggest it?
Noura: My grandmother suggested it when she forgot to drink enough water during a busy afternoon last year.
Interviewer: How will the device work?
Noura: A timer activates a small light and a sound. It never gives medical advice; people still make their own decisions.
Interviewer: Where are the students going to test the prototype, and who is supervising the trial?
Noura: We are going to test it in the science laboratory next month with our teacher and a volunteer engineer.
Interviewer: What happened when you tried an early version, and how are you changing the design because of that problem?
Noura: The warning was too quiet, so we are adding a brighter signal as well as a clearer button.
Interviewer: When is your team meeting the engineer again?
Noura: We are meeting her on Wednesday. The school timetable confirms that she will arrive before the second break.
Interviewer: What advice would you give other students who want to design useful technology for families?
Noura: Ask people what they need, test your ideas carefully and remember that technology should support human judgement.

tasks.title: Reading 2 — Short answers
tasks.passage:
Smart gardens can make school projects more interesting and may help save water. A group of students in Nizwa is developing a garden that uses sensors to measure soil moisture. An app displays the readings, and the class plans to test its first prototype next month. Supporters argue that this kind of technology helps pupils understand how science can solve everyday problems. It also offers practical opportunities to work with measurements and interpret information.

However, there are important disadvantages to consider. A sensor may produce an incorrect result or stop working completely. If students rely only on the app when a sensor breaks, water may be wasted or plants may receive too little. Some classmates therefore worry that automatic watering systems could make people less careful. I agree that a warning from a device should not replace observation of the actual garden.

The class is meeting a local engineer on Tuesday to discuss these risks. Their exhibition will open at nine o'clock on Thursday, and visitors will be able to ask questions about the prototype. One useful improvement would be a manual control that lets pupils stop the irrigation system whenever a reading seems unreliable. The students should also record what happens during several tests rather than trusting one result.

In my opinion, smart technology can help schools when its limits are understood. The group hopes to collect feedback and improve the design before building a larger garden. Its strongest lesson is that technology should be combined with human judgement, accurate evidence and responsible decisions. A successful invention needs careful users, not just clever software.
